name: Mingrelian
confidence_why: Borise 2020 and Poniava 2020 both report that the placement of Megrelian stress is contested, and the first-hand descriptions disagree on where main stress falls in words longer than two syllables: Kipshidze 1914 gives primary initial stress, Kluge 1916 penultimate, Gudava 1969 a penult/antepenult window for the Senaki dialect with contrastive pairs, Kiria, Ezugbaia, Memishishi and Chukhua 2015 the final vowel, and Poniava 2020's 18-speaker acoustic study initial stress in two- and three-syllable words but second-syllable stress in longer ones, so no single rule has a clear winner.

new_statements.quote: Stress properties of Megrelian are contested (though cf. Senaki Megrelian facts in section 4.2). [...] There is agreement in the literature that in disyllabic words stress is initial. Kluge (1916: 3) claims that in longer words stress is penultimate, and accompanied by high tone. According to Kipshidze (1914: 13), longer words have two stresses, primary on the initial syllable and secondary on either the penult (in four syllable words) or the antepenult (in longer ones). Final vowels in Megrelian are often lengthened, especially in the Zugdidi dialect (Gudava 1969: 109), which has also been analyzed as final stress (Tsagareli 1880: 7; Kiziria 1967: 65).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Mingrelian (src StressTyp2) carries an empty rule, so nothing to agree or contradict with; Borise supplies the content: contested placement, initial stress agreed only for disyllables, a penult/antepenult window (C-final = penult, V-final = antepenult) for the Senaki dialect, plus secondary stress and verb-form exceptions.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Borise files Megrelian under 'conflicting descriptions': the only point of agreement is initial stress in disyllables; for longer words the sources diverge (Kluge: penult with high tone; Kipshidze: primary initial + secondary penult/antepenult; Tsagareli/Kiziria: final, which may really be final-vowel lengthening). The one dialect she describes as a system (Senaki, after Gudava 1969, §4.2 p. 8) is a penult/antepenult stress window: penultimate stress in consonant-final words, antepenultimate in vowel-final words, which she groups with quantity-sensitive stress-window systems (fn. 6 compares it to the Greek recessive accent).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Reported second-hand from Kipshidze (1914: 13): primary on the initial syllable, secondary on the penult in four-syllable words and on the antepenult in longer words.
new_statements.exceptions: Senaki dialect (p. 8): some vowel-final verbs, including perfective future and certain aorist forms, keep penultimate stress, giving minimal pairs dóɣuru 'die.AOR.3SG' vs doɣúru 'die.PRF.FUT.3SG' (Gudava 1969: 109). Negative/prohibitive morphemes obligatorily attract stress (p. 11, citing Kluge 1916: 4). Stress is acoustically weak with much interspeaker variation; Samurzakano Megrelian stress is the strongest acoustically (p. 23).
new_statements.identity_note: Borise's stress-window statement is for the Senaki dialect of Megrelian (after Gudava 1969); final-stress analyses concern the Zugdidi dialect (final-vowel lengthening); Samurzakano Megrelian is noted only for acoustically stronger stress. Kluge 1916 and Kipshidze 1914 are not dialect-specified in Borise's summary.

new_statements.quote: 1. Wort-Akzent. Das Haupt-Gesetz: zweisilbige Wörter betonen die erste Silbe, mehrsilbige betonen die vorletzte Silbe; danach richten sich auch alle Lehnwörter. Dieses Gesetz wird durchbrochen und zwar 1. bei der Deklination in allen denjenigen Formen, in denen der Vokal der letzten Silbe ausgefallen ist, also namentlich im Genitiv und Dativ. [...] 2. Bei der Konjugation. [...] β) Präsens und Futurum betonen die letzte Silbe, soweit sie konsonantisch ausgehen, sonst ist das Haupt-Gesetz die Regel. [p. 4:] In der verneinenden Aussageform liegt der Ton auf der ersten Silbe vár-moko „ich will nicht“, bei der fragenden auf der letzten: goko-nó „willst du“
new_statements.translation: 1. Word accent. The main law: disyllabic words stress the first syllable, polysyllabic words stress the penultimate syllable; all loanwords also conform to this. This law is broken (1) in declension, in all those forms in which the vowel of the last syllable has dropped out, i.e. especially in the genitive and dative. [...] (2) In conjugation. [...] (b) Present and future stress the last syllable insofar as they end in a consonant, otherwise the main law is the rule. [p. 4:] In the negative declarative form the accent lies on the first syllable, vár-moko 'I do not want'; in the interrogative on the last: goko-nó 'do you want'.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record is classification excluded with no rule; the one existing statement (Borise 2020) classes Megrelian stress as contested and already cites 'Kluge (1916: 3)' for penultimate stress in longer words. The primary text confirms that attribution exactly (disyllables initial, polysyllables penult, loanwords conform) and adds the full list of morphological exceptions, the negation/interrogative accent shifts (Borise p. 11 cites Kluge 1916: 4 for negation attracting stress -- confirmed: 'vár-moko') and the no-regular-sentence-accent remark. One detail of Borise's paraphrase is NOT in Kluge pp. 3-4: nothing there says penult stress is 'accompanied by high tone' (the nearest 'Ton' passag…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default ('Haupt-Gesetz'): word stress on the penultimate syllable (stated as first syllable in disyllables, penult in longer words, which is the same position); loanwords follow the same law. Morphologically conditioned departures: (i) genitive/dative and other case forms whose final vowel has been elided keep the stress where it was, so it surfaces on the final syllable (koǯêp'iš beside koǯêpiši); disyllabic suffixes attract stress to their own first syllable; (ii) infinitives in -iri, -uala, -umala stress the antepenult (-ua counts as one syllable); (iii) present/future forms ending in a consonant stress the final syllable, otherwise penult; aorist (always vowel-final) mostly penult but trisyllabic forms often stress the augment vowel (k'êp'č'op'i beside gilêp'ši); same for other tenses; (iv) negative verb forms stress the first syllable (vár-moko), interrogative forms the last (goko-nó), negative-interrogative forms both first and last. Sentence accent ('2. Satz-Akzent', p. 4): speech is extremely fast and 'von einem regelmäßigen Akzent kann nicht gesprochen werden'; words given weight in discourse are stressed. p. 2: stressed vowels are held somewhat longer; the vowel ê is always long and always carries the accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such. The only double-accent statement is for negative-interrogative verb forms ('liegt der Ton auf der ersten und letzten Silbe'). Kluge says nothing about a secondary stress in long words (contrast Kipshidze 1914: 13 as reported by Borise 2020 and Poniava 2020) and nothing about high tone accompanying stress in the Akzent section.
new_statements.exceptions: Gen./dat. forms with elided final vowel (stress then final); disyllabic suffixes take stress on the suffix's first syllable ('treten zweisilbige Suffixe an ein Wort, so geht der Ton auf die erste Silbe des Suffixes über'); infinitives in -iri/-uala/-umala antepenult ('-ua wird als eine Silbe behandelt'); consonant-final present/future forms final; trisyllabic aorists often stress the augment (initial); negative forms initial, interrogative final, negative-interrogative first+last; vowel ê always stressed; some 1/2sg present/future forms with an audible final -k'ə syllable may even carry the accent on it (p. 3). Druckfehler p. 94: only a punctuation correction ('Silbe:') in this passage.
new_statements.identity_note: Kluge's material was collected in summer 1912 in Nowo-Senaki (Novo-Senaki, today Senaki; Gouv. Kutais) with the priest Giorgi Gamzardia of the Senaki seminary (Vorwort p. 1), i.e. it describes Senaki Megrelian -- the same variety Borise 2020 §4.2 singles out ('Senaki Megrelian facts'). Kluge notes verb forms differ higher up in the mountains.

tone_statements.translation: Megrelian-Chan stress is mobile, weak dynamic-musical, weaker than in Georgian and Svan. … A. Chikobava has attested in the Atina and Arkabe [Laz] texts a tonal stress whose place is fixed: it is always on the 2nd syllable from the end! The vowel concerned is pronounced lengthened … Not even a remnant of tonal stress is attested in Megrelian. … Interrogative intonation is peculiar: on the last syllable of the last word of an interrogative sentence the tone (voice) is raised: mu ikip? 'what are you doing?'
tone_statements.locator: p. 88 (section 'მახვილი (აქცენტუაცია) კოლხურში'), interrogative-intonation sentence top of p. 89
tone_statements.summary: No tone in Megrelian: stress is weak, mobile, 'dynamic-musical'; the fixed penultimate tonal accent Chikobava found in Atina/Arkabe Laz has no trace in Megrelian; questions raise final-syllable pitch.

readall_conflicts: Borise 2020 (p. 23) herself reports the disagreement: the literature agrees only that disyllables are stressed initially; for longer words Kluge 1916 gives penultimate stress (with high tone), Kipshidze 1914 gives primary initial stress with a secondary stress on the penult (4 syllables) or antepenult (5+), and Tsagareli 1880 / Kiziria 1967 analyse the lengthened final vowel (especially Zugdidi) as final stress; Gudava 1969 for the Senaki dialect gives a penult/antepenult window (penult if consonant-final, antepenult if vowel-final) with verb-form exceptions. Kluge 1916 itself could not be opened, so its claim rests on Borise's paraphrase. Poniava 2020 (already held by the project in the same folder from an earlier reading, not in this work list) adds an experimental result of initial stress in 2-3 syllable words, antepenult in 4-syllable words and second-syllable primary stress with a penult/antepenult secondary in 5-7 syllable words, which again differs from Kluge's penult. The catalog record for Mingrelian (src StressTyp2) carries an empty rule and there are no existing_statements. The secondary literature already held by the project (Borise 2020 §7.2, preprint p. 23) itself states that 'Stress properties of Megrelian are contested': Kluge (1916: 3) is reported as disyllables initial / longer words penultimate with high tone; Kipshidze (1914: 13) as primary initial with secondary on penult or antepenult; Tsagareli 1880 / Kiziria 1967 as final (lengthened final vowels, Zug…

sources.quote: Although the nature of stress in Mingrelian has not been thoroughly studied, the position of stress in one dialect has been carefully analyzed (GUDAVA 1969). On this basis, stress in one Senak subdialect is described below. It must be borne in mind, however, that there is considerable variation in this subdialect, as well as differences between it and other subdialects. The general rule is that in consonant-final words, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable, while in vowel-final words it falls on the pre-penultimate syllable (third from the end): V́C0VC0(V)#. The operation of this rule can be seen in the following contrasts: p’č’árundi ‘I was writing it’ -- p’č’arúndit ‘we were writing it’, ǰoɣórepi ‘dogs-Nom’ -- ǰoɣorépiš ‘dogs-Gen’. In a certain set of vowel-final words, however, stress falls on the penultimate syllable, contrary to the general rule. This occurs primarily in verbs, under one of three conditions [...] Clitics form a phonetic unit with a host, and it is this phonetic unit that determines stress.
sources.locator: §1.3 Stress, pp. 6-7; Negative proclitic bearing stress: vámašu, p. 74 (§3 Syntax, after ex. 105, citing GUDAVA 1969:109)
sources.note: Primary stress rule for one Senak subdialect, taken from Gudava 1969: C-final words penult, V-final words antepenult (V́C0VC0(V)#). Exceptions: a set of V-final words, mainly verbs, take penult stress under three conditions: (1) perfective future of 'passives' (markerless / i--u / a--u intransitives), e.g. doɣúru 's/he will die'; (2) aorists of the type taking screeve marker -e in 1st/2nd person, e.g. mevoɣóre, mioɣóru; (3) a small lexical set, e.g. komíc’u 's/he told me'; Harris attributes these to diachronic syllable-count changes. sources.quote: p. 33 (abstract): 'In the scientific literature there is no common view regarding the position and nature of stress in Megrelian. Our study is based on experimental analysis. The experiment has revealed that in Megrelian, in two-syllable and three-syllable words the stress is on the initial syllable. However, in some case the stress falls on the penultimate syllable in three-syllable words. As for four-syllable words, the stress is on the antepenult though our experiment did not confirm the presence of the secondary stress. In five-syllable words the primary stress falls on the second syllable

sources.note: The only instrumental study of Megrelian word stress (18 speakers, 9 municipalities); states outright that the literature has no common view and finds weak stress with a length-dependent locus (σ1 at 2-3σ, σ2 at 4-7σ) matching none of Kipshidze/Klimov/Gudava/StressTyp2 — the quotable modern authority for the exclusion, which currently carries no quote at all.

tone.quote: მეგრულ-ჭანურის მახვილი მოძრავია, სუსტი დინამიკურ-მუსიკალური, უფრო სუსტი, ვიდრე ქართულსა და სვანურში. … ა. ჩიქობავას ათინურსა და არქაბულ ტექსტებში დადასტურებული აქვს ტონური მახვილი, რომლის ადგილი მტკიცეა, ბოლოდან II მარცვალზეა ყოველთვის! სათანადო ხმოვანი გაგრძელებულად გამოითქმის … ტონური მახვილის ნაშთიც არაა მეგრულში დადასტურებული. … კითხვითი ინტონაცია თავისებურია, კითხვითი წინადადების ბოლო სიტყვის ბოლო მარცვალზე ხდება ტონის (ხმის) აწევა: მუ იქიფ1 „რას აკეთებ?“

tone.translation: Megrelian-Chan stress is mobile, weak dynamic-musical, weaker than in Georgian and Svan. … A. Chikobava has attested in the Atina and Arkabe [Laz] texts a tonal stress whose place is fixed: it is always on the 2nd syllable from the end! The vowel concerned is pronounced lengthened … Not even a remnant of tonal stress is attested in Megrelian. … Interrogative intonation is peculiar: on the last syllable of the last word of an interrogative sentence the tone (voice) is raised: mu ikip? 'what are you doing?'

sources.note: Intonation study only: declaratives start low, end falling (LHL%, rarely HL%); H/L are intonational tones from Praat pitch tracks; nothing on lexical tone; each word said to have its own stress.

tone.quote: The research has revealed that the Megrelian declarative sentence – simple, simple complicated and compound – begins with a low pitch and ends with falling intonation; … even within a sentence, the members gradually fall and rise in tone depending on a speaker’s attitude, i.e. which part of speech they want to focus on. … The Megrelian declarative sentence is mainly characterized by LHL% intonation contour, though HL% intonation contour can also be found in rare cases. … L - Low tone, H - High tone, L% - Low boundary tone.

sources.citation: Shengelia, Eter & Natia Poniava. 2019. Intonation of Interrogative Sentences in Zan (Megrelian-Laz) Language. International Journal of Multilingual Education VII(2) [= no. 14]: 26-35. doi:10.22333/ijme.2019.14004
sources.note: Instrumental (Praat) study of question intonation: wh- and yes/no questions carry stress on the wh-word or verb with a rising terminal contour; the Megrelian interrogative suffix -o attracts stress/rising pitch to the preceding (penultimate) vowel; tag and echo questions rising. Treats word prosody purely as stress plus phrasal intonation; makes no claim of lexical tone. Cites Rogava 1956 and Gudava 1969 on stress.

tone.quote: The material analysis has shown that Megrelian-Laz interrogative sentences have the stress on the wh-word or on the verb; Sometimes non-question word is stressed and has rising intonation as well; negative and positive question tags have rising intonation contour as well as echo questions on the interrogative particle. [...] In Megrelian penultimate vowel is stressed in a three-syllable word (მორთუო? Mortuo? – Has he/she come?’) [see Fig. 4], but in a two-syllable word (ხენო? Xeno? – ‘Is he/she sitting?’) -ო (o) suffix has rising intonation contour

tone.quote: Удвоенія … не слѣдуетъ смѣшивать съ природной долготой звука. Въ послѣднемъ случаѣ, какъ извѣстно, звукъ является цѣльнымъ и непрерывнымъ, имѣющимъ своё удареніе (Lautaccent), или моментъ самой большой интенсивности тона, свойственнаго ему … Въ удвоеніи же мингрельскаго а, какъ и другихъ гласныхъ, чуткое и привычное ухо явственно можетъ различить на мгновеніе наступившую паузу … такъ, что на мгновеніе звукъ какъ бы прерывается, или значительно понижается въ серединѣ т. е. тамъ, гдѣ обыкновенно въ цѣльномъ звукѣ бываетъ мѣсто (зенитъ) самаго высокаго поднятія тона.

tone.translation: Doublings … must not be confused with the natural length of a sound. In the latter case, as is known, the sound is whole and continuous, having its own accent (Lautaccent), or moment of the greatest intensity of tone proper to it … In the doubling of Mingrelian a, as of the other vowels, a sensitive and practised ear can clearly distinguish a momentary pause … so that for a moment the sound is as it were interrupted, or drops considerably in the middle, i.e. where in a whole sound the place (zenith) of the highest raising of tone usually lies.

tone.quote: როგორც ჩანს, ეს გრძელი ხმოვანი არის დინამიკური მახვილის აკუსტიკური შთაბეჭდილება (მახვილიანი ხმოვანი ჩვეულებრივ უფრო გრძელია, ვიდრე უმახვილო [გ. ახვლედიანი, 1949, 122]). ტ. გუდავას აზრით, „მახვილის ადგილი მეგრულში საკმაოდ დაუდეგარია, მნიშვნელოვანი სხვაობა გვაქვს თქმების მიხედვით, ხშირია პარალელური ფორმებიც“ [გუდავა, 1969] [...] ამ წესის მიხედვით მახვილი ფიქსირებული, უძრავი გამოდის მეგრულში (ისევე, როგორც ქართულში) [...] ჭანურ‐მეგრულის მახვილი, ს. ჟღენტის აზრით, მოძრავია.

tone.translation: Evidently this long vowel is the acoustic impression of dynamic stress (a stressed vowel is usually longer than an unstressed one [G. Akhvlediani 1949: 122]). In T. Gudava's opinion, 'the place of stress in Megrelian is rather unstable; there are significant differences between subdialects and parallel forms are frequent' [Gudava 1969] [...] By this rule stress comes out fixed, immobile in Megrelian (just as in Georgian) [...] Chan-Megrelian stress, in S. Zhgenti's opinion, is mobile.
tone.says: Word prosody is treated only as (dynamic) stress: Megrelian long final vowels are 'the acoustic impression of dynamic stress'; vowel length non-phonemic in Zan; stress placement rules after Gudava 1969 (penult in C-final, antepenult in V-final words; unstable across subdialects) vs Zhgenti 1953: 192-193 (mobile, occasional final stress: k'uá 'stone'). No mention of lexical tone or tonal accent anywhere in 1070 pp. (a full-text search for stress/accent ტონ-/მუსიკალ- negative except 'intonational…
